## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with hypertension on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Most notably, the direct enrichment of regulation of blood pressure (Gene Ontology:0008217, p = 1.44 × 10−8, 21 associated proteins) strongly supports the view that the prioritized protein set captures core mechanisms involved in vascular tone, fluid balance, and circulatory homeostasis. This interpretation is further complemented by the phenotype terms hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002615, p = 1.80 × 10−2, 17 proteins) and orthostatic hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0001278, p = 4.53 × 10−2, 9 proteins), which together suggest that many of the same molecular regulators may contribute to blood pressure instability across both hypertensive and hypotensive states. In turn, this pattern is consistent with published work indicating shared involvement of endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and altered vasoactive signaling.

Building on this hemodynamic theme, the enrichment profile also points to a broader inflammatory context that may interact with blood pressure regulation.

A second major theme is inflammation and immune activation. The very strong enrichment of overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WikiPathways:5095, p = 4.22 × 10−18, 39 proteins), neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p = 7.35 × 10−15, 67 proteins), and signaling by interleukins (Reactome:R-HSA-449147, p = 3.66 × 10−8, 53 proteins) indicates that inflammatory cytokine networks and innate immune cell activation are central features of the hypertension-associated signature. This interpretation agrees with a large body of literature showing that interleukin signaling, leukocyte recruitment, and neutrophil-derived proteases and oxidants can promote endothelial injury, vascular stiffness, renal sodium retention, and sustained elevation of arterial pressure. The enrichment of viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, p = 7.44 × 10−20, 35 proteins) further reinforces the apparent importance of cytokine-receptor systems, even though this pathway is annotated in an infectious context.

Taken together, these immune-related signals appear to connect naturally with structural changes in the vessel wall and surrounding tissue environment.

A third prominent component involves extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue fibrosis. External encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p = 4.46 × 10−39, 93 proteins), collagen metabolic process (Gene Ontology:0032963, p = 2.91 × 10−9, 18 proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p = 4.63 × 10−15, 34 proteins), and carbohydrate binding (Gene Ontology:0030246, p = 5.06 × 10−15, 29 proteins) together point to marked alterations in matrix composition, proteoglycan interactions, and cell-surface adhesion biology. These findings are highly relevant because vascular fibrosis, collagen accumulation, and remodeling of the arterial wall are well-established contributors to increased vascular resistance and reduced compliance in hypertension. The associated enrichment of lysosome (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04142, p = 1.41 × 10−9, 28 proteins) also fits with prior literature linking lysosomal processing to inflammatory turnover, matrix degradation, and vascular remodeling.

Beyond these broadly shared vascular and inflammatory processes, the dataset also contains tissue-enriched signals that may reflect more specialized biological contexts.

Finally, tissue-enriched signals from placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (Human Protein Atlas:0381223, p = 6.13 × 10−7, 26 proteins) and duodenum; endocrine cells[greater than or equal to Low] (Human Protein Atlas:0151291, p = 2.99 × 10−7, 50 proteins) may reflect specialized secretory and barrier-associated proteins that participate in endocrine, inflammatory, and vascular regulation. The placental signal is particularly notable in light of the established relationship between placental dysfunction, endothelial injury, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, whereas the endocrine cell signal may point more tentatively to hormone-mediated regulation of vascular and metabolic homeostasis. Overall, the pathway pattern supports a model in which hypertension may arise from the convergence of blood pressure regulatory mechanisms, chronic inflammation, cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tissue-specific endocrine or vascular responses, with many of these enrichments showing very strong statistical support across 18 to 93 associated proteins.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (HPA:0381223) 

The pathway described as placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[high] refers to the highly specialized apical surface of syncytiotrophoblasts that lines the chorionic villi of the placenta and is densely covered by microvilli. This microvillous membrane forms the principal maternal-facing exchange interface of the placenta and is essential for nutrient uptake, ion transport, peptide handling, endocrine signaling, barrier integrity, and communication between the placenta and the maternal circulation. Because syncytiotrophoblasts are directly exposed to maternal blood, their microvilli are not only structural amplifiers of surface area but also active signaling platforms enriched in membrane proteins, cytoskeletal components, glycocalyx molecules, and extracellular vesicle release machinery. The cited literature indicates that this compartment is highly sensitive to placental ischemia, oxidative stress, and abnormal trophoblast differentiation in hypertensive pregnancy. Earlier ultrastructural studies showed that placentas from pregnancies complicated by hypertension display reduced microvillar density, decreased intramembranous particles, reduced actin content in the microvillar cytoskeleton, and other features interpreted as syncytiotrophoblast immaturity or injury, changes likely to impair maternal-fetal exchange and membrane signaling (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:2792915, PubMed:6754249). Additional work demonstrated increased lipid peroxidation in syncytiotrophoblast microvillous plasma membranes in pregnancy-induced hypertension, supporting the view that oxidative damage to this membrane domain contributes to placental dysfunction and maternal vascular injury (PubMed:8035780). More recent evidence extends this concept from morphology to mechanism by showing that syncytiotrophoblast-derived extracellular vesicles carry pathogenic cargo, including neprilysin, from the placental surface into the maternal circulation, where they can directly impair vasodilatory signaling and induce preeclamptic hypertension (PubMed:40304042). Reduced syndecan-1 expression on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli in preeclampsia further suggests disturbance of the placental glycocalyx at this surface, linking microvillous injury to altered maternal vascular adaptation (PubMed:27299886).

Taken together, these observations provide a useful framework for interpreting why this placental surface compartment may be relevant to hypertension-associated molecular enrichment.

The collected publications support a model in which the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous pathway is closely linked to hypertension in pregnancy because this placental surface is both a target of placental stress and a source of factors that drive maternal vascular dysfunction. Classical morphologic studies consistently reported that hypertensive placentas show fewer syncytiotrophoblast microvilli, lower actin content, reduced intramembranous particles, basement membrane thickening, syncytial injury, and other signs of structural immaturity or ischemic damage, indicating that the maternal-facing trophoblast surface is profoundly altered in hypertensive disease (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:6754249, PubMed:2792915). These abnormalities are functionally important because loss or simplification of microvilli reduces exchange capacity and likely disrupts membrane-associated signaling between placenta and mother. Oxidative injury appears to be one major mechanism: microvillous plasma membranes from pregnancy-induced hypertension contain increased lipid peroxidation products and show enhanced susceptibility to oxidative stress, a state that could favor release of damaging placental factors into the maternal circulation and amplify endothelial dysfunction and vasoconstriction (PubMed:8035780). The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from the recent study showing that syncytiotrophoblasts are the predominant placental source of neprilysin, which is increased in extracellular vesicles derived from preeclamptic placentas; these vesicles enter maternal endothelial cells, degrade C-type natriuretic peptide, suppress natriuretic peptide receptor-B-mediated cyclic guanosine monophosphate production in adjacent vascular smooth muscle cells, impair uterine arterial vasodilation, and induce hypertension and proteinuria in experimental models, thereby directly connecting the syncytiotrophoblast surface compartment to the hypertensive phenotype (PubMed:40304042). In parallel, reduced syndecan-1 on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli before and during preeclampsia indicates disruption of the glycocalyx on this maternal-facing surface, and its inverse association with systolic blood pressure further supports the relevance of microvillous integrity to blood pressure regulation in pregnancy (PubMed:27299886). Broader reviews of preeclampsia also place syncytiotrophoblast stress, endothelial activation, abnormal placental signaling, and disturbed natriuretic peptide biology at the center of disease pathogenesis, which is consistent with the view that injury to the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous pathway contributes to the development and maintenance of hypertension by coupling placental malperfusion to systemic maternal vascular dysfunction (PubMed:38586611).[PubMed:40304042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40304042) [PubMed:2627339](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2627339) [PubMed:2635867](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2635867) [PubMed:8035780](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8035780) [PubMed:38586611](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38586611) [PubMed:6754249](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6754249) [PubMed:2792915](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2792915) [PubMed:27299886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27299886) 

With this biological context in place, the enrichment result can be interpreted more coherently in relation to the published structural and mechanistic evidence.

There were 26 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[high]. This placental surface domain represents the principal maternal-facing exchange interface, and the enrichment of 26 proteins in this compartment is highly consistent with the established biology of hypertensive pregnancy, in which structural, oxidative, and signaling abnormalities converge at the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous membrane. The pathway description indicates that this membrane is essential for nutrient uptake, ion transport, peptide handling, endocrine signaling, barrier maintenance, and communication with the maternal circulation, thereby linking a single highly specialized placental surface to multiple disease-relevant processes. In hypertension, this relevance is supported by several independent lines of evidence showing reduced microvillar density, decreased intramembranous particles, diminished actin content, and broader features of syncytiotrophoblast immaturity or injury in affected placentas (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:2792915, PubMed:6754249). Additional evidence for pathogenic involvement comes from increased lipid peroxidation in syncytiotrophoblast microvillous plasma membranes in pregnancy-induced hypertension, quantitatively reinforcing the interpretation that oxidative injury at this maternal-facing membrane contributes to placental dysfunction and maternal vascular damage (PubMed:8035780). Mechanistic extension of these observations further shows that syncytiotrophoblast-derived extracellular vesicles can transfer pathogenic cargo, including neprilysin, into the maternal circulation and directly impair vasodilatory signaling, thereby promoting hypertensive pathology (PubMed:40304042). Reduced syndecan-1 expression on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli in preeclampsia adds another layer of evidence, suggesting that disturbance of the placental glycocalyx at this surface is linked to abnormal maternal vascular adaptation (PubMed:27299886). Collectively, the enrichment of 26 proteins in this pathway provides a quantitatively focused and biologically coherent signal that hypertension-associated molecular changes are concentrated at a placental membrane domain already implicated by ultrastructural, biochemical, and mechanistic studies.

To further contextualize these 26 proteins, the interaction network below provides a visual overview of their potential functional connectivity.

The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network for these 26 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

Building on this network-level view, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified in the function enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a more gene-specific manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

NOS3 stands out as the protein with the clearest and most direct relevance to hypertension because endothelial nitric oxide is a central determinant of vascular tone, arterial compliance, and blood pressure homeostasis. The provided annotation indicates that VEGF receptor signaling promotes phosphorylation of NOS3 and induces NO production in endothelial cells, while also regulating endothelial survival, permeability, and cytoskeletal organization. These processes are highly pertinent to hypertension, which is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, vascular remodeling, and altered microvascular integrity. Reduced NOS3 activity or impaired upstream activation can diminish NO bioavailability, thereby increasing vasoconstriction, promoting inflammation and platelet-endothelial interactions, and facilitating structural vascular changes that sustain elevated blood pressure. Thus, among the listed proteins, NOS3 is the strongest mechanistic link to hypertension pathogenesis through its role in endothelial signaling and NO-dependent vascular regulation.

From vascular tone regulation, it is then logical to consider proteins that may influence the contractile apparatus of the vessel wall itself.

ACTA2 is highly relevant to hypertension because smooth muscle alpha-actin is a core structural component of vascular smooth muscle cells, which determine arterial tone and vessel wall remodeling. Although the provided description is general, actin-dependent contractility and cytoskeletal dynamics are fundamentally involved in vasoconstriction, mechanotransduction, and the adaptive or maladaptive remodeling of resistance arteries in chronic hypertension. Increased vascular smooth muscle contractile activity and structural stiffening are major contributors to elevated peripheral resistance, the principal hemodynamic abnormality in essential hypertension. Therefore, ACTA2 is notable as a cytoskeletal effector that may connect cellular motility and contractile architecture to hypertensive vascular remodeling and increased arterial stiffness.

In addition to vascular contractility, endothelial handling of oxidative and lipid-related stress may also be relevant to the hypertensive state.

COLEC12 is of particular interest in hypertension because its endothelial scavenger receptor function links vascular inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid handling. The annotation specifically notes its role in recognition, internalization, and degradation of oxidatively modified low-density lipoprotein by vascular endothelial cells. Oxidative stress and oxidized low-density lipoprotein accumulation are central features of endothelial injury and vascular inflammation, both of which contribute to reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, increased vascular stiffness, and remodeling in hypertension. Through its ability to sense modified lipids and participate in endothelial clearance pathways, COLEC12 may influence the inflammatory vascular milieu that promotes hypertensive target-organ damage and accelerates atherosclerotic complications commonly associated with high blood pressure.

A closely related consideration involves enzymes that may limit the accumulation of oxidatively damaged membrane lipids.

PLA2G15 is relevant to hypertension because phospholipid remodeling and detoxification of oxidized phospholipids are closely tied to vascular oxidative stress and inflammatory injury. The annotation highlights its ability to selectively hydrolyze truncated oxidized phospholipids and suggests a role in detoxification during oxidative stress. This is mechanistically important because oxidized phospholipids can damage endothelial cells, amplify inflammatory signaling, and impair vasodilatory responses, all of which are central to hypertensive vascular dysfunction. In addition, its broader role in membrane lipid homeostasis and intracellular lipid trafficking may influence macrophage and endothelial cell responses in cardiometabolic disease states that frequently coexist with hypertension. Hence, PLA2G15 may be a meaningful contributor to vascular injury pathways rather than a direct regulator of blood pressure itself.[PubMed:10092508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10092508) [PubMed:11790796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790796) [PubMed:20410020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20410020) [PubMed:23958596](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23958596) [PubMed:25727495](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25727495) [PubMed:29724779](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29724779) [PubMed:30830753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830753) [PubMed:36823305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) 

Beyond oxidative and lipid injury, several enriched proteins may be relevant through inflammatory and immune-mediated mechanisms.

FCN1 is noteworthy because it connects innate immune activation, complement signaling, and monocyte inflammatory responses to hypertension-related vascular disease. Chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a driver of endothelial dysfunction, arterial remodeling, and hypertensive end-organ injury. The ability of FCN1 to activate the complement lectin pathway and stimulate monocytes to secrete interleukin 8 suggests a plausible role in promoting vascular inflammation, leukocyte recruitment, and endothelial activation. While FCN1 is not a classical blood pressure regulator, its immunologic functions may be especially relevant in inflammatory or metabolic forms of hypertension, where innate immune signaling contributes to persistent vascular dysfunction.

This inflammatory theme is further extended by proteins that may restrain, rather than amplify, immune activation.

LAIR1 is potentially important in hypertension because it functions as a broad suppressor of immune-cell activation and inflammatory cytokine production. Hypertension is now widely understood to have an immune component, involving T-cell activation, cytokine-mediated vascular dysfunction, and inflammatory injury in the kidney and vasculature. The annotation indicates that LAIR1 down-regulates interleukin 2, interferon gamma, interleukin 8, interleukin 10, and tumor necrosis factor-related pathways and inhibits nuclear factor kappa B signaling, all of which are highly relevant to inflammatory amplification in hypertensive disease. Consequently, LAIR1 may represent a protective immunoregulatory axis whose reduced activity could permit excessive vascular and renal inflammation, thereby facilitating blood pressure elevation and tissue damage.

Related to this, leukocyte movement across the vascular barrier may provide another route by which immune activation contributes to hypertensive tissue injury.

CD99L2 is relevant because leukocyte transmigration across the endothelium is a key event in vascular inflammation, which contributes to endothelial dysfunction and remodeling in hypertension. The annotation specifically places CD99L2 at a late step of leukocyte extravasation, facilitating passage through the endothelial basement membrane. This function could be important in hypertensive target-organ damage, where infiltration of inflammatory cells into vascular, renal, and cardiac tissues promotes fibrosis, oxidative stress, and structural remodeling. Although CD99L2 is not a direct regulator of vascular tone, it may contribute to the inflammatory tissue environment that sustains chronic hypertension and its complications.

At a broader immunologic level, antigen presentation pathways may also shape adaptive immune responses relevant to hypertensive disease.

CD74 may have an indirect but meaningful connection to hypertension through antigen presentation and adaptive immune activation. The role of CD74 in major histocompatibility complex class two processing places it upstream of T-cell-mediated immune responses, and adaptive immunity has been implicated in the development and maintenance of hypertension, especially in relation to vascular inflammation and renal injury. Enhanced antigen presentation can promote pro-inflammatory T-cell activation, which in turn may impair endothelial function, increase oxidative stress, and contribute to sodium-retaining and vasoconstrictive states. Therefore, CD74 is relevant as part of the immunologic machinery that could shape inflammatory hypertension phenotypes.

In addition to these vascular and immune-related proteins, systemic stress-response mediators may also be informative in this enriched set.

GDF15 is of interest because it is a systemic stress signal with strong links to cardiometabolic regulation, energy balance, and disease severity. Although the annotation focuses on the GDF15-GFRAL axis in the brainstem, its induction by stressors such as cancer, drugs, and metabolic perturbation suggests broader relevance to hypertension, particularly in obesity-associated or systemic inflammatory states. Appetite suppression, altered lipid metabolism, and stress-response signaling may influence body weight, insulin sensitivity, and vascular risk, all of which modulate blood pressure. Thus, GDF15 is better viewed as a biomarker and systemic mediator of cardiometabolic stress that may accompany or modify hypertension rather than as a primary vascular effector.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) 

Finally, lipid transport and lipoprotein-associated vascular protection may provide an additional layer of contextual relevance.

APOD is potentially relevant to hypertension because high-density lipoprotein metabolism is closely related to vascular protection, oxidative balance, and endothelial health. By stabilizing high-density lipoprotein structure and influencing high-density lipoprotein metabolism, APOD may affect reverse cholesterol transport and the anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative properties of lipoproteins. These functions are important in the context of hypertension, where endothelial dysfunction and vascular stiffness are often exacerbated by dyslipidemia and oxidative stress. Although APOD is not a direct regulator of blood pressure, it may modify the vascular risk environment in which hypertension develops and contributes to cardiovascular complications.

### Hypotension (HP:0002615) 

Hypotension, or abnormally low arterial blood pressure, is a hemodynamic state in which systemic perfusion pressure becomes insufficient to maintain adequate blood flow during rest, postural change, meals, anesthesia, or other physiological stressors. In vascular hypotension, the central biological problem is failure to preserve effective blood pressure through the coordinated actions of cardiac output, intravascular volume, peripheral vascular resistance, autonomic reflexes, renal sodium handling, and neurohumoral regulation. A major clinical form is orthostatic hypotension, defined by an excessive fall in blood pressure after standing, which may arise from autonomic failure, impaired baroreflex compensation, volume depletion, medication effects, or cardiovascular dysfunction. Contemporary work further recognizes distinct hemodynamic patterns such as initial orthostatic hypotension, delayed blood pressure recovery, classic orthostatic hypotension, and delayed orthostatic hypotension, emphasizing that hypotension is not a single entity but rather a spectrum of disorders with heterogeneous mechanisms and prognostic implications. Importantly, hypotension often coexists with hypertension rather than representing its simple opposite. This coexistence is especially evident in older adults, people with chronic kidney disease, patients with autonomic disorders, and individuals receiving antihypertensive therapy. In these settings, the same patient may exhibit elevated supine or seated blood pressure together with impaired blood pressure maintenance during standing, sleep, or perioperative stress. Taken together, the hypotension pathway may be understood most coherently as a disorder of blood pressure regulation and instability, linking autonomic dysfunction, vascular stiffness, impaired reflex buffering, medication exposure, and end organ perfusion abnormalities.  

Against this physiological background, the provided literature suggests that the hypotension pathway is closely and bidirectionally related to hypertension, because both conditions arise from dysregulation of blood pressure control and frequently coexist in the same individual rather than occurring as isolated opposites. Several reviews and scientific statements emphasize that orthostatic hypotension is a common comorbidity of hypertension, particularly in older adults and in those with autonomic impairment, and that management must balance the risks of cerebral and systemic hypoperfusion against the long-term harms of elevated resting blood pressure and supine hypertension (PubMed:38205630, PubMed:33881284, PubMed:35841911). This relationship appears clinically important because orthostatic hypotension in hypertensive populations is associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including stroke, heart failure, and broader cardiovascular risk, as shown in chronic kidney disease cohorts and in trial populations with hypertension-related kidney disease (PubMed:33851116, PubMed:30354704). At the same time, supine hypertension, which commonly accompanies neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does not appear benign; it has been associated with renal dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, cerebral white matter injury, cardiovascular events, falls, and increased mortality, suggesting that attempts to correct standing hypotension while overlooking elevated supine pressure may worsen hypertensive target organ damage (PubMed:32516630, PubMed:30882602, PubMed:37646155). Evidence from randomized trial analyses further indicates that intensive blood pressure treatment does not generally increase orthostatic hypotension risk enough to negate cardiovascular benefit, suggesting that the presence of orthostatic hypotension alone should not automatically preclude antihypertensive treatment, although treatment choice remains important because some drug classes, such as beta blockers and long-acting renin angiotensin system inhibitors, may increase susceptibility to hypotensive episodes in selected settings (PubMed:37847274, PubMed:30354704, PubMed:36368916). The connection is also evident in perioperative medicine, where chronic hypertension and abnormal circadian blood pressure regulation predict postinduction and intraoperative hypotension, indicating that longstanding hypertension may impair vascular and autonomic adaptability and thereby predispose patients to acute low-pressure states during physiological stress (PubMed:35306353, PubMed:35139104). Collectively, these studies support the view that the hypotension pathway is mechanistically embedded within hypertension disease through shared determinants including autonomic dysfunction, vascular stiffness, medication exposure, kidney disease, and impaired baroreflex buffering, and that both low and high blood pressure contribute to morbidity, requiring individualized management that addresses blood pressure variability across body position, time of day, and treatment context.[PubMed:38205630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38205630) [PubMed:33881284](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33881284) [PubMed:35841911](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35841911) [PubMed:33851116](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33851116) [PubMed:30354704](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30354704) [PubMed:32516630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32516630) [PubMed:30882602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30882602) [PubMed:37646155](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37646155) [PubMed:37847274](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37847274) [PubMed:36368916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36368916) [PubMed:35306353](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35306353) [PubMed:35139104](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35139104) 

Building on this clinical and mechanistic context, the enrichment results provide a more focused view of how this pathway may intersect with hypertension-related biology. There were 17 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing hypotension, or abnormally low arterial blood pressure, indicating that this functional category captures a quantitatively defined subset of the hypertension-related protein set. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway centers on dysregulated blood pressure maintenance through altered cardiac output, intravascular volume, peripheral vascular resistance, autonomic reflex control, renal sodium handling, neurohumoral regulation, and end-organ perfusion, all of which are highly relevant to the instability of blood pressure observed in hypertension. The coexistence of hypertension with hypotensive states, particularly orthostatic blood pressure decline and impaired hemodynamic compensation, further supports the interpretation that these 17 proteins may be linked not simply to elevated pressure alone, but also to broader failures in blood pressure regulation across different physiological conditions and stress responses. With this network-level overview in place, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and consider their possible relevance in a more detailed and ordered manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, REN has the most direct and established mechanistic connection to hypertension. Renin is the rate-limiting initiator of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, a central endocrine axis controlling vascular tone, extracellular fluid volume, and sodium homeostasis. By cleaving angiotensinogen to angiotensin one, renin triggers downstream generation of angiotensin two, a potent vasoconstrictor that also stimulates aldosterone secretion, enhances tubular sodium reabsorption, and contributes to vascular remodeling. Dysregulation of this pathway is a canonical driver of essential and secondary hypertension, and the clinical importance of REN is underscored by the widespread use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system-targeting therapies in hypertensive disease. Therefore, REN appears to stand out as the strongest hypertension-relevant protein in this list because it lies at the apex of a pathway that directly determines blood pressure set point.  

Closely related to REN in the same regulatory axis, ACE is also highly relevant to hypertension because angiotensin-converting enzyme is a core effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, where the somatic enzyme classically converts angiotensin one to angiotensin two and thereby promotes vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sodium retention, and blood pressure elevation. While the supplied description focuses mainly on the testis-specific isoform and male fertility, it explicitly notes the existence of distinct somatic isoforms, which is important because the somatic enzyme is the clinically relevant form in cardiovascular regulation. The inability of testis-specific and somatic isoforms to fully compensate for one another further supports functional specialization. In the context of hypertension, ACE is a major disease gene and therapeutic target, as excessive angiotensin-converting enzyme-dependent angiotensin two generation contributes not only to elevated blood pressure but also to endothelial dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and renal injury. Thus, despite the reproductive emphasis in the annotation, ACE remains one of the most important proteins in this list for hypertension biology.[PubMed:1651914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1651914) [PubMed:9482924](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482924) [PubMed:16270063](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16270063) [PubMed:10831599](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10831599) [PubMed:11723129](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11723129) [PubMed:12777443](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12777443) [PubMed:9664078](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9664078) [PubMed:15665832](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15665832) 

Moving from direct endocrine regulation to metabolic and inflammatory influences, LEP is strongly relevant to hypertension because it links adiposity, metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and cardiovascular regulation. In obesity, hyperleptinemia is common and is thought to contribute to obesity-associated hypertension through multiple mechanisms, including increased sympathetic nervous system activity, vascular effects, low-grade inflammation, and altered renal sodium handling. The annotation highlights leptin's broad endocrine and immunomodulatory actions, including effects on hypothalamic circuits controlling energy expenditure, pro-inflammatory signaling, angiogenesis, and endothelial biology. These functions are highly pertinent to hypertensive disease, particularly in the setting of metabolic syndrome, where leptin can act as a pathogenic mediator connecting excess adipose tissue to elevated blood pressure, vascular remodeling, and target-organ injury. Its activation of Janus kinase two signal transducer and activator of transcription three, phosphoinositide three kinase, and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways further supports a mechanistic role in vascular and inflammatory processes that frequently accompany hypertension.[PubMed:11373681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11373681) [PubMed:12594516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12594516) [PubMed:15899045](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15899045) [PubMed:16825198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16825198) [PubMed:20620997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20620997) [PubMed:10660043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10660043) [PubMed:25060689](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25060689) [PubMed:25383904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25383904) [PubMed:8589726](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8589726) [PubMed:9732873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9732873) 

In addition to these regulators of pressure control and metabolic signaling, several matrix-related proteins may be relevant because hypertension is also associated with structural remodeling of the vessel wall and target organs. COL1A1 is indirectly but meaningfully related to hypertension through its role in extracellular matrix organization and tissue fibrosis. Hypertension is not only a hemodynamic disorder but also a structural disease characterized by vascular stiffening, arterial wall remodeling, and fibrosis in the heart and kidney. Type one collagen is a major determinant of matrix accumulation in these processes. Increased deposition of COL1A1-containing fibrils can reduce vascular compliance, increase pulse wave velocity, and exacerbate systolic hypertension. In hypertensive target organs, excessive type one collagen is also associated with myocardial fibrosis and progressive nephrosclerosis. Although COL1A1 is not a primary blood pressure regulator like REN or ACE, it appears to be an important downstream effector of chronic hypertensive injury and a marker of maladaptive remodeling.  

A related extracellular matrix perspective is provided by COL5A1, which may be relevant to hypertension through its contribution to extracellular matrix architecture and vessel wall properties. Type five collagen participates in fibrillogenesis and influences the organization of collagen fibers, thereby affecting tissue tensile strength and compliance. In hypertension, altered extracellular matrix composition contributes to arterial stiffness and vascular remodeling, both of which sustain elevated blood pressure and promote end-organ damage. The reported binding interactions of type five collagen with heparan sulfate and thrombospondin further suggest potential relevance to matrix signaling and vascular biology. Although the connection is more indirect than for renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system components, COL5A1 stands out as a plausible modifier of hypertensive vascular remodeling.  

Shifting from matrix biology to receptor-mediated signaling, KIT has a less direct but potentially relevant connection to hypertension through growth factor signaling, vascular cell biology, and receptor turnover. The annotation emphasizes post-translational regulation of KIT by suppressor of cytokine signaling-dependent ubiquitination, which may influence the intensity and duration of KIT signaling. Because KIT participates in cell survival, proliferation, and progenitor cell functions, altered KIT activity could affect vascular remodeling, endothelial repair, and inflammatory cell behavior, all of which are relevant to hypertensive vascular disease. However, compared with REN, ACE, and LEP, the evidence from the provided annotation is more circumstantial. KIT is therefore better viewed as a potentially contributory signaling regulator rather than a core hypertension gene in this dataset.  

Finally, at the level of cellular stress adaptation and protein synthesis, EIF4G1 is not a classical hypertension gene, but its role in translational control may be relevant to cellular stress responses implicated in hypertensive organ damage. The annotation specifically notes a requirement for endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced activating transcription factor four translation, which is notable because endoplasmic reticulum stress and integrated stress responses have been implicated in endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and cardiac and renal remodeling in hypertension. Thus, EIF4G1 may influence how vascular or renal cells adapt to hypertensive stress at the level of protein synthesis. Nonetheless, based on the supplied information, the connection appears mechanistically plausible rather than direct.

### Duodenum; endocrine cells[≥Low] (HPA:0151291) 

The pathway described as duodenum endocrine cells refers to the specialized enteroendocrine cell population embedded within the duodenal mucosa. These cells act as nutrient, neural, and humoral sensors and release peptide mediators that coordinate digestion, glucose handling, appetite, autonomic output, vascular tone, and fluid and electrolyte balance. Although the duodenum is classically viewed as part of the digestive tract, its endocrine compartment is increasingly recognized as a systemic regulatory interface linking the gut to the cardiovascular, renal, metabolic, and neuroendocrine systems. Duodenal endocrine cells produce or participate in the regulation of hormones and neuropeptides such as ghrelin, glucagon-like peptide related signals, and cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript related peptides, all of which can influence sympathetic activity, energy homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory tone, and vascular responses. In the context of hypertension, this pathway is biologically relevant because alterations in duodenal endocrine cell number, phenotype, or secretory activity may modify gut-derived hormonal signaling to the kidney, vasculature, heart, and central autonomic nuclei. Thus, the duodenal endocrine cell pathway can be viewed as a component of the broader gut cardiovascular axis through which gastrointestinal endocrine remodeling may contribute to blood pressure dysregulation and hypertensive end-organ injury.

Building on this biological framework, the available literature suggests a relationship between duodenal endocrine cells and hypertension primarily through evidence that hypertension is accompanied by remodeling of gastrointestinal endocrine signaling and by plausible downstream effects of gut-derived hormones on cardiovascular control. The most direct evidence comes from renovascular hypertension models showing that ghrelin-immunoreactive endocrine cells are increased in the duodenum of hypertensive rats, indicating that elevated blood pressure or the associated renal and neurohumoral disturbances alter the endocrine architecture of the proximal small intestine; the authors further suggested that altered ghrelin secretion may contribute to cardiovascular complications in hypertension (PubMed:27966210). Complementing this observation, another study demonstrated that hypertension increases cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript positive structures in the gastrointestinal tract, including neuroendocrine elements in the small intestine, supporting the concept that hypertension is associated with broader gastrointestinal neuroendocrine plasticity rather than an isolated change in a single hormone system (PubMed:22887004). These findings are important because gut endocrine mediators can influence appetite, adiposity, insulin action, sympathetic tone, and inflammatory pathways, all of which are mechanistically linked to blood pressure elevation. This interpretation is further supported indirectly by review evidence showing that obesity-related renal disease extends beyond hypertension and insulin resistance through endocrine and inflammatory signaling between metabolic tissues and the kidney, highlighting how peripheral endocrine networks may aggravate renal injury and thereby sustain hypertensive disease (PubMed:36726470). In addition, experimental work in metabolic disease models indicates that gut-related endocrine signals such as glucagon-like peptide associated pathways participate in pancreatic and systemic metabolic regulation, which is relevant because disturbed metabolic homeostasis strongly interacts with hypertension pathogenesis (PubMed:29186652). Taken together, the literature suggests that the duodenal endocrine cell pathway is related to hypertension not because it is a classic primary blood pressure pathway, but because hypertension induces measurable changes in duodenal endocrine cell populations, and these changes may feed back through gut hormone signaling to influence cardiovascular regulation, renal function, metabolic balance, and the progression of hypertensive complications.[PubMed:27966210](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27966210) [PubMed:22887004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22887004) [PubMed:36726470](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36726470) [PubMed:29186652](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29186652) 

To complement the literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides a quantitative view of the pathway-level signal. There were 50 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as duodenum endocrine cells, indicating a quantitatively substantial signal that links this gastrointestinal endocrine regulatory compartment to blood pressure control, vascular reactivity, metabolic coordination, autonomic regulation, and fluid and electrolyte homeostasis. This protein count of 50 supports the interpretation that the enrichment is not driven by an isolated molecular event but instead reflects a broader systems-level convergence between gut-derived endocrine signaling and hypertension biology, particularly through mechanisms involving peptide mediator release, sympathetic modulation, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory balance, renal communication, and cardiovascular end-organ responses. Many of these proteins are therefore likely to participate in the gut cardiovascular axis through which altered duodenal endocrine cell function, abundance, or secretory phenotype may contribute to blood pressure dysregulation and hypertensive tissue injury. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 50 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/557f4bd4-576c-490d-a50d-c14c3b0f522f.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=38A91B603BDE1695)

With this network-level context in place, several significant proteins identified during the functional enrichment analysis can be discussed in greater detail. We will introduce them in detail in the following.

DDAH1 is one of the most directly relevant proteins in this list for hypertension because it controls the bioavailability of nitric oxide, a central determinant of vascular tone, endothelial function, and blood pressure homeostasis. By degrading asymmetric dimethylarginine and monomethylarginine, DDAH1 relieves inhibition of nitric oxide synthase and promotes nitric oxide production. Reduced nitric oxide signaling is a well-established mechanism contributing to endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, arterial stiffness, and elevated peripheral resistance, all of which are fundamental features of hypertension. Therefore, altered DDAH1 activity could plausibly influence hypertensive disease by modulating the balance between vasodilation and vasoconstriction. Among the proteins listed, this represents one of the clearest mechanistic links to blood pressure regulation.

In parallel with this vascular regulatory mechanism, immune and inflammatory control may also be relevant within the enriched protein set. CFI is notable because dysregulated complement activation is increasingly implicated in vascular inflammation, endothelial injury, renal damage, and thrombotic microangiopathic processes that can contribute to hypertension, particularly secondary and inflammation-associated forms. By inactivating C3b and C4b, CFI protects host tissues from excessive complement-mediated injury. This function is especially relevant to hypertension because chronic low-grade inflammation and endothelial damage are major contributors to vascular remodeling and renal dysfunction, both of which sustain elevated blood pressure. In the kidney, inadequate control of complement activation may promote glomerular and microvascular injury, impair sodium handling, and accelerate progression toward hypertensive end-organ damage. Thus, CFI stands out as an immune-regulatory protein with a plausible role in the inflammatory vascular and renal mechanisms underlying hypertension.[PubMed:17320177](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17320177) [PubMed:7360115](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7360115) [PubMed:12055245](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12055245) [PubMed:2141838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2141838) [PubMed:9605165](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9605165) [PubMed:28671664](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28671664) 

Extending this inflammatory perspective, IL18 is highly relevant to hypertension because inflammation is now recognized as a major driver of vascular dysfunction, renal injury, and target-organ remodeling. IL18 promotes nuclear factor kappa B-dependent inflammatory signaling and amplifies T helper 1 and natural killer cell responses, linking innate and adaptive immunity. These processes are pertinent to hypertension, where inflammatory cytokines contribute to endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, vascular stiffening, and renal sodium-retaining states. The association of IL18 with pyroptosis is particularly interesting, as inflammasome activation and inflammatory cell death have emerged as mechanisms that can exacerbate vascular and renal injury in cardiometabolic disease. Consequently, IL18 may connect immune activation to the chronic low-grade inflammation that characterizes many forms of hypertension and hypertensive organ damage.[PubMed:26638072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638072) [PubMed:26638073](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638073) [PubMed:30392956](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30392956) 

Closely related to this theme, GCHFR is of particular interest because it links danger sensing to non-canonical NLRP3 inflammasome activation, a pathway increasingly associated with cardiovascular inflammation and hypertension. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome can promote release of inflammatory mediators, endothelial dysfunction, and tissue injury in both the vasculature and kidney. Given that hypertension is strongly influenced by sterile inflammation and innate immune activation, a protein that facilitates inflammasome assembly may have meaningful pathophysiological relevance. The described ability of GCHFR to respond to mitochondrial deoxyribonucleic acid released during pyroptosis is also notable, as mitochondrial stress and inflammatory cell death are both implicated in hypertensive vascular remodeling and renal damage. Thus, GCHFR stands out as a plausible upstream regulator of inflammatory mechanisms that may worsen blood pressure control.

Shifting from inflammatory regulation to lipid mediator biology, ADH4 is especially noteworthy because of its activity toward 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid, a bioactive eicosanoid with well-established effects on vascular tone, renal tubular transport, and blood pressure regulation. 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid can promote vasoconstriction and influence sodium handling, and dysregulation of its synthesis or degradation has been repeatedly linked to hypertension. By oxidizing 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid and related omega-hydroxy fatty acids, ADH4 may participate in the metabolic clearance or transformation of a lipid mediator that is highly relevant to hypertensive physiology. Its additional role in retinoid metabolism may also be relevant, given that retinoid signaling can affect vascular and metabolic homeostasis. Overall, ADH4 stands out because it intersects directly with eicosanoid pathways that are mechanistically tied to renal and vascular contributors to hypertension.[PubMed:17279314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17279314) [PubMed:16081420](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16081420) 

Along the same general line of lipid mediator control, PTGR1 is relevant to hypertension because it modulates prostaglandin metabolism, and prostaglandins are important regulators of vascular tone, renal blood flow, and sodium excretion. Altered prostaglandin balance can shift the vasodilatory-constrictive equilibrium and thereby influence blood pressure. In addition, the reported repression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma activity is potentially important, since peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma has protective roles in vascular biology, insulin sensitivity, and anti-inflammatory signaling; impaired peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma signaling is often associated with metabolic syndrome and hypertension. Therefore, PTGR1 may connect eicosanoid metabolism with cardiometabolic mechanisms that predispose to elevated blood pressure, particularly in obesity-associated or inflammation-associated hypertension.

A broader metabolic layer is also suggested by FABP1. FABP1 is relevant to hypertension through its central role in hepatic lipid handling and systemic metabolic homeostasis. Dyslipidemia, ectopic lipid accumulation, and broader metabolic syndrome are major contributors to endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and increased arterial stiffness, all of which promote hypertension. By facilitating intracellular transport of fatty acids and cholesterol, FABP1 may influence circulating lipid profiles and hepatic metabolic responses that indirectly affect vascular health. Although its connection to blood pressure is less direct than that of DDAH1 or ADH4, FABP1 stands out as a plausible contributor to the metabolic milieu that often accompanies and aggravates hypertension.

Continuing this metabolic interpretation, FBP1 is of interest in hypertension because it sits at the intersection of glucose metabolism, insulin physiology, adiposity, and energy balance. These processes are highly relevant to the development of obesity-related hypertension and the broader cardiometabolic syndrome. Excess hepatic gluconeogenesis and impaired insulin sensitivity promote hyperglycemia, endothelial dysfunction, renal sodium retention, and sympathetic activation, all of which can elevate blood pressure. The reported effects of FBP1 on appetite and adiposity further strengthen its relevance, as obesity is a major risk factor for hypertension. Thus, FBP1 may contribute indirectly but meaningfully to hypertensive disease through metabolic pathways that shape vascular and renal stress.

Within the same cardiometabolic context, KHK is a particularly interesting metabolic candidate because fructose metabolism has been strongly linked to hypertension in experimental and epidemiological contexts. By catalyzing the first committed step of fructose utilization, KHK promotes downstream metabolic effects that can include adenosine triphosphate depletion, uric acid generation, oxidative stress, insulin resistance, and lipogenesis. These changes can impair endothelial function, enhance renal sodium retention, and contribute to vascular dysfunction, thereby increasing blood pressure. Although the entry provided here is concise, the biological role of KHK places it squarely within pathways that are frequently implicated in diet-associated and metabolic hypertension.

A related connection to systemic metabolic dysfunction is provided by CES1. CES1 may be relevant to hypertension because it participates in adipose lipid metabolism, a key determinant of systemic metabolic health. Disturbances in adipose lipolysis and lipid turnover contribute to obesity, insulin resistance, ectopic fat deposition, and inflammatory signaling, all of which are strongly linked to elevated blood pressure. As a major lipase in white adipose tissue, CES1 could influence the release and handling of lipid species that affect vascular reactivity and metabolic homeostasis. Its additional involvement in retinyl ester metabolism may also have indirect implications for transcriptional and metabolic regulation. Therefore, CES1 is best viewed as a candidate connecting adipose dysfunction to cardiometabolic forms of hypertension.[PubMed:15220344](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220344) 

Beyond metabolic regulation, the enriched set also points toward vascular structural remodeling. COL18A1 is relevant because endothelial homeostasis and microvascular integrity are central to blood pressure regulation. Its anti-angiogenic activity, classically associated with the endostatin domain, suggests a role in controlling vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling. In hypertension, microvascular rarefaction, impaired endothelial repair, and abnormal angiogenic balance contribute to increased peripheral resistance and target-organ ischemia. By modulating vascular endothelial growth factor A-kinase insert domain receptor signaling and integrin-dependent endothelial migration, COL18A1 may influence vascular remodeling processes that are important in chronic hypertension. This makes it a notable extracellular matrix-related regulator of the vascular phenotype.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

In addition to structural vascular effects, fibrotic and inflammatory tissue remodeling may also be relevant. LGALS3 is one of the more compelling candidates because galectin-3 is widely associated with inflammation, fibrosis, and adverse cardiovascular remodeling. The functions listed here support its role as a multifunctional mediator of innate immunity and tissue response to injury. These properties are highly relevant to hypertension, particularly because chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling in the heart, vessels, and kidney are major determinants of disease progression and end-organ damage. Through effects on leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, and inflammatory activation, LGALS3 may contribute to vascular stiffening and renal interstitial injury. Its role in damage sensing and autophagy regulation further suggests a capacity to influence cellular stress responses in hypertensive tissues.

Finally, the protein set also includes a candidate with potential relevance to renal transport organization and vascular protection. PDZK1 is notable because it links membrane transporter organization with lipid metabolism and renal tubular physiology, both of which are relevant to hypertension. Its role in maintaining scavenger receptor class B member 1 expression suggests an influence on high-density lipoprotein-related cholesterol handling and vascular protection, whereas its regulation of proximal tubular transport proteins implicates it in renal electrolyte homeostasis. Since the kidney is central to long-term blood pressure control, proteins that affect transporter localization in the proximal tubule may alter sodium and anion handling and thereby affect extracellular volume and blood pressure. PDZK1 therefore stands out as a plausible modulator of both vascular risk and renal mechanisms contributing to hypertension.

### Orthostatic hypotension (HP:0001278) 

Orthostatic hypotension is a disorder of blood pressure regulation in which blood pressure falls excessively after transition from lying or sitting to standing. This phenomenon reflects failure of the integrated compensatory responses that normally preserve cerebral and systemic perfusion during orthostasis, including baroreflex activation, sympathetic vasoconstriction, heart rate adjustment, and maintenance of venous return. Contemporary clinical literature indicates that orthostatic hypotension is not a single uniform entity, but rather a heterogeneous hemodynamic syndrome with several patterns, including initial orthostatic hypotension, delayed blood pressure recovery, classic orthostatic hypotension, and delayed orthostatic hypotension, each with distinct temporal features and clinical implications. The condition may be neurogenic, as in autonomic failure associated with synucleinopathies, diabetic neuropathy, or other neurological disorders, or non-neurogenic, as in volume depletion, medication effects, cardiovascular deconditioning, and age-related impairment in vascular and autonomic responsiveness. Clinical manifestations range from dizziness, visual blurring, fatigue, cognitive slowing, presyncope, syncope, and unexplained falls to asymptomatic blood pressure drops detectable only by measurement. In older adults, orthostatic hypotension is especially important because it frequently coexists with frailty, polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, falls, and functional decline. A particularly important variant is the coexistence of orthostatic hypotension with supine hypertension, in which blood pressure is elevated while lying down but falls markedly on standing, creating a paradoxical pattern of blood pressure instability that complicates diagnosis and treatment. Management is therefore individualized and usually begins with careful characterization of posture-related blood pressure changes, identification of provoking medications and comorbidities, nonpharmacological strategies, and selective use of short-acting pressor or antihypertensive therapies depending on whether upright symptoms or nocturnal and supine hypertension predominate.  

Against this physiological and clinical background, the relationship between orthostatic hypotension and hypertension appears especially close, bidirectional, and clinically important because both disorders arise from impaired blood pressure regulation rather than representing completely separate conditions. In older adults, hypertension and orthostatic hypotension commonly coexist, with shared contributions from arterial stiffness, impaired baroreflex buffering, autonomic dysfunction, and medication exposure, making blood pressure control difficult and often unstable across body positions and time of day (PubMed:39717228, PubMed:38205630). Evidence from randomized trial analyses indicates that the presence of orthostatic hypotension should not automatically be interpreted as a reason to avoid antihypertensive treatment, because more intensive blood pressure lowering or active treatment reduced cardiovascular disease events or mortality to a similar extent in participants with and without baseline orthostatic hypotension, and intensive treatment generally did not increase orthostatic hypotension risk in major hypertension trials (PubMed:37847274, PubMed:30354704, PubMed:30715100). At the same time, orthostatic hypotension itself identifies a higher-risk hypertensive phenotype, being associated with stroke, nonfatal cardiovascular disease, falls, fractures, dementia, functional impairment, and mortality in selected populations, including people with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and older age (PubMed:30354704, PubMed:32675475, PubMed:30715100). The association is further complicated by the fact that some antihypertensive or cardiovascular drug classes can unmask or worsen orthostatic blood pressure decline in susceptible patients, with reports implicating beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, antidepressants, sedatives, and other agents in specific cohorts, although risk appears to vary by population and formulation (PubMed:23855394, PubMed:39528998, PubMed:32009474, PubMed:38205630). A major mechanistic and therapeutic intersection between orthostatic hypotension and hypertension is the syndrome of supine hypertension with orthostatic hypotension, especially in neurogenic autonomic failure, in which elevated blood pressure while supine contributes to nocturnal sodium loss, worsened daytime orthostatic intolerance, and long-term target organ injury involving the heart, kidneys, and brain, while treatment of upright hypotension may aggravate supine hypertension and treatment of supine hypertension may worsen standing symptoms (PubMed:35841911, PubMed:30882602, PubMed:33687577, PubMed:33058087, PubMed:32516630, PubMed:35230654, PubMed:36601916). Thus, orthostatic hypotension is related to hypertension not merely as an adverse effect of therapy, but as a manifestation of dysregulated cardiovascular homeostasis that modifies risk assessment, influences antihypertensive drug selection, and necessitates individualized management balancing prevention of cardiovascular and renal complications against preservation of upright perfusion and fall prevention.[PubMed:39717228](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39717228) [PubMed:37847274](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37847274) [PubMed:35841911](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35841911) [PubMed:23855394](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23855394) [PubMed:28050656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28050656) [PubMed:30882602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30882602) [PubMed:33687577](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33687577) [PubMed:33058087](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33058087) [PubMed:32675475](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32675475) [PubMed:32516630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32516630) [PubMed:32009474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32009474) [PubMed:30715100](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30715100) [PubMed:30354704](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30354704) [PubMed:31524637](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31524637) [PubMed:39528998](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39528998) [PubMed:38205630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38205630) [PubMed:36601916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36601916) [PubMed:35230654](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35230654) 

Building on this clinical framework, the enrichment results suggest that orthostatic hypotension may also intersect with hypertension at the molecular level. There were 9 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing orthostatic hypotension as a disorder of blood pressure regulation in which blood pressure falls excessively after transition from lying or sitting to standing. This pathway captures a quantitatively important hemodynamic phenotype defined by impaired compensatory control of cerebral and systemic perfusion during orthostasis, including altered baroreflex activation, sympathetic vasoconstriction, heart rate adjustment, and preservation of venous return, and it further reflects the clinical heterogeneity of the condition across initial orthostatic hypotension, delayed blood pressure recovery, classic orthostatic hypotension, and delayed orthostatic hypotension, as well as neurogenic and non-neurogenic forms that are highly relevant to hypertension because of their shared disturbances in vascular tone, autonomic responsiveness, volume status, medication effects, and the frequent coexistence of supine hypertension with marked standing blood pressure decline.

To place these 9 proteins into a network context, the interaction analysis is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 9 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration and evidence review.

![PPI Network](imgs/40f2de5d-2b19-47dd-a137-65d0aab47e6d.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=067634EFDBF12C90)

With this network view in mind, the following section introduces the proteins highlighted by the functional enrichment analysis in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the proteins listed, LEP stands out as the most directly and mechanistically relevant to hypertension. Leptin is centrally involved in obesity-related cardiometabolic dysfunction, a major driver of elevated blood pressure. Its hypothalamic actions on appetite and energy expenditure connect it to obesity, which is a well-established risk factor for hypertension. Beyond body weight regulation, leptin has important peripheral vascular and inflammatory effects that are highly pertinent to hypertensive disease. It is described as pro-angiogenic and mitogenic for endothelial cells, and as a regulator of matrix remodeling through modulation of MMPs and TIMPs, suggesting a role in vascular structural adaptation and stiffness, both of which contribute to increased peripheral resistance. LEP also activates JAK2-STAT3, PI3K, MAP2K1/MEK1, and MAPK14/p38 signaling and promotes pro-inflammatory mediator production, including IL6 and IL8, indicating that it may contribute to the chronic low-grade inflammation and endothelial dysfunction frequently observed in hypertension. Its effects on innate and adaptive immunity further strengthen this link, because immune activation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to vascular injury and blood pressure elevation. Collectively, the metabolic, vascular, inflammatory, and remodeling functions of leptin make it a particularly compelling candidate for involvement in hypertension pathogenesis, especially in obesity-associated and inflammation-associated forms of the disease.[PubMed:11373681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11373681) [PubMed:12594516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12594516) [PubMed:15899045](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15899045) [PubMed:16825198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16825198) [PubMed:20620997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20620997) [PubMed:10660043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10660043) [PubMed:25060689](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25060689) [PubMed:25383904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25383904) [PubMed:8589726](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8589726) [PubMed:9732873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9732873) 

A related but distinct line of reasoning concerns extracellular matrix structure and tissue mechanics, which may also be relevant to sustained blood pressure elevation. COL1A1 is highly relevant to hypertension because type I collagen is a principal determinant of extracellular matrix composition and tissue mechanical properties. Although the provided annotation is concise, the biological importance of fibrillar collagen strongly suggests a connection to vascular remodeling, arterial stiffness, and fibrosis, which are central pathological features of chronic hypertension. Excessive deposition of type I collagen in the vascular wall can reduce arterial compliance, increase pulse wave velocity, and elevate systolic blood pressure. In addition, collagen accumulation in the heart and kidney is commonly associated with hypertensive end-organ damage, including myocardial fibrosis and nephrosclerosis. Therefore, even though no direct hypertension-specific citation is included in the supplied description, COL1A1 stands out because extracellular matrix expansion and stiffening are core mechanisms in the development and maintenance of elevated vascular resistance.  

Extending this extracellular matrix perspective, COL5A1 may also warrant consideration as a potential modifier of vascular structural properties. COL5A1 is potentially relevant to hypertension because type V collagen participates in connective tissue organization and likely influences extracellular matrix assembly together with other fibrillar collagens. Its ability to interact with heparan sulfate, thrombospondin, heparin, and insulin suggests possible roles in matrix-cell signaling, growth factor availability, and vascular wall structure. In the context of hypertension, extracellular matrix disorganization and altered collagen composition contribute to vascular stiffening and maladaptive remodeling. Although COL5A1 is a minor collagen component, such molecules can exert disproportionate effects on fibril architecture and tissue integrity. Therefore, COL5A1 may be of interest as a modifier of vascular extracellular matrix properties that could influence arterial compliance and susceptibility to hypertensive remodeling, even if the supplied annotation does not provide direct disease-specific evidence.  

Finally, in contrast to the more structural and metabolic candidates discussed above, EIF4G1 appears to have a more indirect and stress-response-related connection to hypertension. EIF4G1 is less directly connected to hypertension than LEP or the collagen genes, but it remains biologically interesting because it regulates translational control, including translation during endoplasmic reticulum stress via ATF4. Endoplasmic reticulum stress and maladaptive stress-response signaling have been implicated in vascular dysfunction, inflammation, and hypertensive end-organ injury. Through its role in selective messenger ribonucleic acid translation, EIF4G1 could influence how vascular, renal, or metabolic cells respond to stress conditions relevant to hypertension. However, based on the information provided, the connection is indirect and currently more mechanistic than disease-specific. Thus, EIF4G1 is best regarded as a potential upstream regulator of stress-adaptive pathways rather than a primary hypertension effector in this protein set.

### Spinal cord injury (WP:WP2431) 

Spinal cord injury is a pathological state initiated by traumatic or perioperative damage to the spinal cord, followed by persistent neurological, vascular, immune, endocrine, and metabolic consequences. In the context of cardiovascular regulation, the spinal cord is not merely a conduit for descending motor and sensory signals, but also a critical integrative structure for autonomic control of vascular tone, cardiac function, and reflex blood pressure regulation. Injury, particularly at or above the major thoracic sympathetic outflow, interrupts supraspinal inhibitory and modulatory control over sympathetic preganglionic circuits. This disruption produces a chronic state of autonomic instability in which patients may experience both sustained blood pressure abnormalities and episodic hypertensive crises triggered by otherwise innocuous stimuli below the lesion, such as bladder distension, bowel care, pain, or clinical urodynamic testing. Experimental studies further indicate that spinal cord injury induces maladaptive structural and functional plasticity within spinal sympathetic networks, including excitatory interneuron remodeling, enhanced noradrenergic signaling, and inflammatory signaling driven in part by soluble tumor necrosis factor alpha, all of which may amplify sympathetic reflexes and promote pathological pressor responses. In parallel, spinal cord injury is associated with broader cardiometabolic dysregulation, including adipose tissue dysfunction, abnormal lipolysis, ectopic lipid deposition, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, which may contribute to long-term vascular risk. Clinical cohort data further indicate that traumatic spinal cord injury is associated with increased long-term incidence of hypertension, stroke, and coronary artery disease, supporting the view that spinal cord injury is a systemic disease state with substantial relevance to blood pressure control and hypertensive vascular injury.

Building on this physiological framework, the collected literature indicates that spinal cord injury is strongly linked to hypertension through both chronic and episodic mechanisms centered on autonomic dysregulation. At the population level, traumatic spinal cord injury confers a significantly increased long-term risk of developing hypertension, with hazard ratios of approximately 1.5 to 1.6 across independent health system cohorts, and postinjury hypertension is also associated with increased mortality, indicating that hypertension is not merely coincidental but a clinically important sequela of spinal cord injury itself (PubMed:41186949). Mechanistically, high-level spinal cord injury removes descending control over sympathetic circuits and permits maladaptive reorganization of spinal autonomic networks, creating exaggerated reflex sympathetic discharge in response to sensory input below the lesion. This process underlies autonomic dysreflexia, a syndrome of sudden uncontrolled hypertension that is repeatedly described as a life-threatening complication after injury above the sixth thoracic level (PubMed:40963010, PubMed:35304427, PubMed:36381835). Experimental work has shown that thoracic excitatory spinal interneurons drive structural remodeling of sympathetic pathways after injury and thereby increase the frequency and severity of hypertensive episodes, while inhibition of these neurons reduces dysautonomia and autonomic dysreflexia (PubMed:35304427). In parallel, persistent soluble tumor necrosis factor alpha signaling promotes sympathetic hyperreflexia, and delayed intrathecal blockade attenuates autonomic dysreflexia for months, supporting a causal role for inflammatory remodeling in postinjury hypertension (PubMed:31754014). Clinical studies further demonstrate that common procedures such as urodynamic testing can provoke profound blood pressure surges, with systolic arterial pressure exceeding 200 millimeters of mercury in autonomically complete injuries, emphasizing that hypertension after spinal cord injury is often stimulus-evoked, severe, and arrhythmogenic rather than simply essential hypertension in a disabled population (PubMed:36187786). Additional evidence suggests that pain can trigger hypertensive episodes after spinal cord injury and that interventions such as propofol or spinal cord stimulation can reduce these responses, again implicating aberrant sensory autonomic coupling in blood pressure elevation (PubMed:40166966, PubMed:39238671). Beyond direct autonomic mechanisms, spinal cord injury also promotes cardiometabolic states linked to hypertension, including dyslipidemia, diabetes, adipose tissue dysfunction, and physical deconditioning; sensory plasticity in adipose-innervating pathways has been shown experimentally to disturb lipid handling after injury, offering a plausible route by which spinal cord injury may further increase chronic vascular risk (PubMed:38663398, PubMed:39517327). Taken together, these studies support the interpretation that spinal cord injury may contribute to hypertension by disrupting central autonomic regulation, inducing maladaptive sympathetic plasticity and inflammatory signaling, precipitating recurrent hypertensive crises through autonomic dysreflexia, and fostering long-term metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidity.[PubMed:41186949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41186949) [PubMed:40963010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40963010) [PubMed:31754014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31754014) [PubMed:35304427](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35304427) [PubMed:36187786](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36187786) [PubMed:38663398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38663398) [PubMed:39517327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39517327) [PubMed:40166966](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40166966) [PubMed:36381835](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36381835) [PubMed:39238671](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39238671) 

To extend this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides a complementary molecular view of how this pathway may relate to hypertension. There were 19 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing spinal cord injury as a pathological state that disrupts autonomic cardiovascular regulation, vascular control, immune signaling, endocrine balance, and metabolic homeostasis, thereby linking traumatic or perioperative spinal cord damage to sustained blood pressure dysregulation, episodic hypertensive responses, and increased long-term vascular risk.
